title: The brachial plexus
summary: Roots to terminal branches, and what each lesion looks like at the bedside.

steps.title: The whole plexus at once
steps.text:
Five roots (C5–T1) become three trunks behind the clavicle, six divisions, three cords named for their position around the axillary artery, and five terminal branches. Say it once as Real Texans Drink Cold Beer and you have the order for life.

Everything else in this lesson hangs off that skeleton.

steps.title: Roots and trunks in the neck
steps.text:
The roots emerge between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius – the interscalene groove you feel just behind the lower sternocleidomastoid, and where an interscalene block is placed.

C5 and C6 join to make the upper trunk; C7 continues alone as the middle trunk; C8 and T1 join as the lower trunk, which sits on the first rib right behind the subclavian artery.

check.q: Between which two muscles do the roots of the plexus emerge?
check.a: Scalenus anterior and scalenus medius.

steps.title: Upper trunk injury – Erb palsy
steps.text:
A violent increase in the angle between head and shoulder – a fall, or traction at birth – tears C5–C6 at Erb's point.

You lose abduction (deltoid, supraspinatus), lateral rotation (infraspinatus), elbow flexion and supination (biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis). The arm hangs adducted and medially rotated with the forearm pronated: the waiter's tip position.

steps.title: Lower trunk injury – Klumpke palsy
steps.text:
Traction with the arm above the head damages C8–T1. Those roots supply all the small muscles of the hand, so the hand claws: the long flexors are unopposed by the interossei and lumbricals.

T1 also carries the sympathetic outflow to the head, so a very proximal lesion adds a Horner syndrome – ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis.

steps.title: Terminal branches
steps.text: Musculocutaneous pierces coracobrachialis and supplies the anterior arm. Axillary hooks round the surgical neck of the humerus – at risk in shoulder dislocation and in a badly placed deltoid injection. Radial spirals down the radial groove. Median crosses the cubital fossa and enters the carpal tunnel. Ulnar passes behind the medial epicondyle, where you can feel it.

check.q: Which terminal branch winds round the surgical neck of the humerus?
check.a: The axillary nerve.

steps.title: Divisions sort fibres by the side of the limb
steps.text:
Each trunk divides into an anterior and a posterior division. The three posterior divisions join to form the posterior cord, which gives the axillary and radial nerves. These pathways chiefly serve the developing extensor side of the limb.

The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord. They contribute to musculocutaneous, median and ulnar pathways. Follow roots to trunks before following divisions: a cord contains fibres from several spinal levels, not one segment renamed.

check.q: Which divisions form the posterior cord?
check.a: The posterior divisions of all three trunks.

steps.pitfall: Lateral, medial and posterior name the cords relative to the axillary artery, not relative to the vertebral column.

objectives: Recite the plexus from roots to terminal branches
Locate each part in the neck, behind the clavicle and in the axilla
Predict the deficit from an upper or lower trunk injury
Use the anterior and posterior divisions to explain how plexus fibres reach flexor and extensor compartments
takeaways: Real Texans Drink Cold Beer: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches.
Erb's palsy (C5–C6) gives the waiter's tip; Klumpke's (C8–T1) gives a claw hand.
The cords are named for their position around the axillary artery.
All three posterior divisions form the posterior cord; the anterior divisions form the lateral and medial cords.

title: The rotator cuff
summary: Four muscles, one tendon sleeve, and why supraspinatus is always the one that tears.

steps.title: Four muscles, one sleeve
steps.text: Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor and Subscapularis blend with the shoulder capsule to hold the humeral head against a very shallow glenoid. The joint trades stability for range, and the cuff is what pays for it.

check.q: Name the four rotator cuff muscles.
check.a: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis.

steps.title: Supraspinatus and the painful arc
steps.text:
Supraspinatus runs from the supraspinous fossa under the acromion to the greater tubercle. That subacromial passage is a tunnel, and the tendon is squeezed in it during abduction between roughly 60° and 120° – the painful arc of impingement.

Its blood supply is also poorest at the critical zone about 1 cm from the insertion, which is exactly where degenerate tears start.

check.q: Why does supraspinatus tear more often than the others?
check.a: It passes through the narrow subacromial space and has a relatively avascular zone near its insertion.

steps.title: External rotators
steps.text: Infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate. Test them with the arm at the side and the elbow flexed: resisted external rotation. Weakness plus a positive external rotation lag sign suggests a posterosuperior cuff tear.

check.q: Which two cuff muscles laterally rotate the shoulder?
check.a: Infraspinatus and teres minor.

steps.title: Subscapularis, the only one in front
steps.text:
Subscapularis fills the anterior surface of the scapula and inserts on the lesser tubercle; it is the only medial rotator of the four, and the only one anterior to the joint. It is tested by the lift-off and belly-press tests.

Being the anterior wall of the joint, it is the structure torn in anterior dislocation.

check.q: Which cuff muscle medially rotates the arm, and how do you test it?
check.a: Subscapularis — the lift-off or belly-press test.

steps.title: Dissect down to it
steps.text: Peel the deltoid away and the cuff appears. Drag the dissection slider yourself and watch the deltoid and trapezius disappear before the cuff does – exactly the order you would cut in.

steps.title: A force couple keeps the ball centred
steps.text:
Deltoid does not pull only in the direction of rotation: part of its force tends to translate the humeral head upwards. The rotator cuff compresses the head into the glenoid and balances that translation, letting deltoid turn the humerus around a stable centre.

Across the joint, subscapularis in front balances the posterior cuff behind. This is why the cuff works as a coordinated sleeve, not just four separate movement labels. A large tear can break that balance and make active elevation difficult despite an intact deltoid and axillary nerve.

check.q: Why can a major cuff tear impair elevation even if deltoid still contracts?
check.a: The humeral head may no longer remain centred against the glenoid, so deltoid loses the stable pivot needed for efficient elevation.

objectives: Name the four cuff muscles, their attachments and actions
Explain how the cuff stabilises the glenohumeral joint
Say why supraspinatus is the tendon that fails
Explain how cuff compression balances the upward pull of deltoid
takeaways: SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.
The cuff pulls the humeral head into the glenoid so deltoid can abduct against a fixed fulcrum.
Supraspinatus passes through a narrow subacromial space and has a hypovascular zone.
The cuff centres the humeral head during deltoid-driven elevation; a large tear can impair elevation even when deltoid is innervated.

title: The carpal tunnel
summary: Nine tendons and one nerve in a box that cannot expand.

steps.title: The floor and the roof
steps.text: The carpal bones form a concave gutter; the flexor retinaculum roofs it over between the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium laterally and the pisiform and hook of hamate medially. The result is a closed osseofibrous tunnel that cannot stretch.

check.q: What forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?
check.a: The flexor retinaculum, between the scaphoid and trapezium laterally and the pisiform and hook of hamate medially.

steps.title: What is inside
steps.text:
Ten things: four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus, and the median nerve.

What is not inside matters just as much: flexor carpi radialis has its own compartment, and the ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon's canal.

check.q: How many tendons pass through the carpal tunnel, and which nerve?
check.a: Nine tendons — four FDS, four FDP and flexor pollicis longus — with the median nerve.

steps.title: Why the palm is spared
steps.text: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves the trunk 5 cm above the wrist and passes over the retinaculum. In carpal tunnel syndrome the palm therefore keeps its sensation while the lateral three and a half digits go numb – a discriminator from a more proximal median lesion.

check.q: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
check.a: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the tunnel and passes over the retinaculum.

steps.title: Thenar wasting
steps.text:
The recurrent motor branch supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and flexor pollicis brevis. Long-standing compression wastes the thenar eminence and abolishes true opposition; the patient compensates with adductor pollicis, which is ulnar-supplied.

Division of the retinaculum decompresses the tunnel – the reason the operation works at all.

check.q: Which muscles waste in a long-standing median nerve compression at the wrist?
check.a: The thenar muscles — abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and flexor pollicis brevis.

steps.title: Work backwards from the muscles that still work
steps.text:
The median nerve gives off its forearm motor branches before entering the tunnel. Flexor pollicis longus and the lateral part of flexor digitorum profundus receive fibres through the anterior interosseous branch. A lesion confined to the wrist does not disconnect those muscles.

That gives you a useful localisation rule. Thenar weakness with preserved thumb-tip and index-fingertip flexion is compatible with a distal median lesion. Weakness of those long flexors suggests a more proximal motor pathway problem as well. Map a branch point before interpreting a muscle deficit; do not make the wrist responsible for muscles supplied above it.

check.q: Should an isolated carpal tunnel lesion paralyse flexor pollicis longus?
check.a: No. Its anterior interosseous motor supply branches off in the forearm, proximal to the tunnel.

steps.title: A narrow passage can crowd without a fracture
steps.text:
The retinaculum and carpal gutter form a space containing tendons, their synovial coverings and the median nerve. The contents need to glide, but the boundaries have limited ability to expand. Increased volume of the contents can therefore raise pressure even while every bone remains in place.

This connects the anatomy to the pattern of symptoms: the nerve can become compressed while the long flexor tendons remain continuous and still move the fingers. Tendon movement and normal-looking bone alignment do not by themselves establish that the median nerve has enough room.

check.q: Why can finger flexion remain possible despite symptoms from the carpal tunnel?
check.a: The tendons may remain intact and mobile while increased pressure within the tunnel affects the median nerve.

objectives: Name the boundaries and contents of the carpal tunnel
Explain the sensory sparing of the palm in carpal tunnel syndrome
Describe the tests used to confirm it
Use forearm muscle function to distinguish a wrist-level median lesion from a more proximal lesion
takeaways: Nine tendons and the median nerve pass through; the ulnar nerve does not.
The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel, so the palm is spared.
Thenar wasting is a late and important sign.
A lesion confined to the carpal tunnel leaves median-innervated forearm muscles intact because their branches arose proximally.

title: The cubital fossa
summary: The triangle you put a needle into, and what you must not hit.

steps.title: The boundaries
steps.text: A triangle: above, a line between the epicondyles; laterally, brachioradialis; medially, pronator teres. The floor is brachialis and supinator, the roof the deep fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis.

check.q: Name the boundaries of the cubital fossa.
check.a: Pronator teres medially, brachioradialis laterally, and an imaginary line between the epicondyles above.

steps.title: Contents, lateral to medial
steps.text:
Radial nerve (just outside, under brachioradialis), Biceps tendon, Brachial artery, Median nerve – Really Need Beer To Be At My Nicest if you prefer.

The bicipital aponeurosis sweeps medially over the artery, which is why it is called the grace of God tendon: it protects the artery from a needle aimed at the median cubital vein.

check.q: What are the contents from lateral to medial?
check.a: Radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve.

steps.title: The veins on the roof
steps.text: The median cubital vein runs across the roof, joining cephalic to basilic. It is the standard site for venepuncture precisely because the aponeurosis lies between it and the brachial artery.

check.q: Which structure protects the brachial artery from a needle in the fossa?
check.a: The bicipital aponeurosis.

steps.title: The lateral edge leads to a nerve fork
steps.text:
The radial nerve approaches the front of the lateral elbow beneath brachioradialis. Near this border of the fossa it divides into a superficial branch, mainly sensory, and a deep branch, mainly motor. The deep branch passes through supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.

This fork explains why a distal motor lesion can impair finger extension while leaving cutaneous sensation intact. By contrast, a radial nerve lesion before the division can affect both motor and sensory fibres. The cubital fossa is a transition between compartments as well as a place to memorise a list of contents.

check.q: Why can posterior interosseous nerve injury cause motor weakness without a numb patch of skin?
check.a: Cutaneous sensory fibres have already taken the separate superficial radial branch.

steps.title: Roof, contents, floor
steps.text:
Reconstruct the fossa from superficial to deep. Superficial veins lie in the tissue above the deep fascia. The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces that roof, while the brachial artery and median nerve lie deeper. Brachialis and supinator form the muscular floor.

A diagram viewed from the front flattens these layers onto one page, so a vein and artery may appear to cross directly. The 3D relationship is the lesson: crossing in the image is not the same as sharing a depth. Use the aponeurosis as the divider between the superficial venous route and the deeper neurovascular contents.

check.q: Which sheet separates much of the superficial venous roof from the brachial artery and median nerve?
check.a: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforcing the deep fascia.

steps.pitfall: The aponeurosis is an anatomical relationship, not a guarantee that a needle cannot reach a deeper structure.

objectives: Give the boundaries and contents of the cubital fossa
Name the structures at risk during venepuncture
Describe the course of the median nerve through it
Follow the radial nerve as it divides into a superficial sensory branch and a deep motor branch near the elbow
takeaways: Contents from lateral to medial: radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.
The bicipital aponeurosis separates the median cubital vein from the artery beneath.
The roof carries the superficial veins; the floor is brachialis and supinator.
Near the lateral cubital fossa, the radial nerve divides; its deep branch traverses supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.

title: The femoral triangle
summary: NAVEL, the femoral sheath, and where a hernia comes through.

steps.title: The triangle
steps.text: Above: the inguinal ligament. Laterally: the medial border of sartorius. Medially: the medial border of adductor longus. The floor is iliopsoas and pectineus, stepped like a shallow trough; the roof is fascia lata pierced by the saphenous opening.

check.q: What forms the three boundaries of the femoral triangle?
check.a: Inguinal ligament above, sartorius laterally, adductor longus medially.

steps.title: NAVEL
steps.text:
From lateral to medial: femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (the femoral canal with its lymphatics), Lymph node of Cloquet.

Only the artery, vein and canal lie inside the femoral sheath – the nerve is outside it, which is why a femoral nerve block and a femoral line are placed at different points.

check.q: Give the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial.
check.a: Femoral nerve, artery, vein, empty space and lymphatics — NAVEL.

steps.title: The femoral canal and femoral hernia
steps.text:
The medial compartment of the sheath is almost empty – it exists so the vein can expand. Its opening, the femoral ring, is bounded by the inguinal ligament in front, the pectineal ligament behind, the lacunar ligament medially and the vein laterally.

A femoral hernia descends through this rigid ring, so it strangulates readily. It appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; an inguinal hernia is above and medial.

check.q: Why does a femoral hernia strangulate so readily?
check.a: The femoral ring is narrow and bounded by the sharp lacunar ligament medially.

steps.title: Follow it into the adductor canal
steps.text:
At the apex of the triangle the vessels disappear under sartorius into the adductor (subsartorial) canal, between vastus medialis and the adductors. They leave it through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus to become popliteal vessels.

The saphenous nerve travels with them but does not go through the hiatus – it pierces the roof and continues down the medial leg.

check.q: Which three structures run in the adductor canal?
check.a: Femoral artery, femoral vein and the saphenous nerve.

steps.title: Two midpoints with different ends
steps.text:
The inguinal ligament runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. Its midpoint is halfway between those two landmarks. The mid-inguinal point instead lies halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

Because the pubic tubercle lies lateral to the symphysis, these are different points. The femoral artery passes deep to the ligament near the mid-inguinal point. The deep inguinal ring is described relative to the midpoint of the ligament. Tiny differences in landmark wording can therefore move you from a vessel to a canal.

check.q: Which medial landmark is used to locate the mid-inguinal point?
check.a: The pubic symphysis; the pubic tubercle is used for the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.

steps.title: The sheath ends, the vessels continue
steps.text:
The femoral sheath is a short fascial sleeve carried down from the abdominal wall around the proximal femoral vessels. Its three compartments contain artery, vein and the medial femoral canal. It does not accompany the vessels all the way through the thigh.

Below it, the artery and vein continue through the triangle towards the adductor canal. The femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath and soon divides into branches. Keep the sheath and adductor canal separate: one is a short sleeve just below the inguinal ligament; the other is a longer muscular passage farther down the thigh.

check.q: Are the femoral sheath and adductor canal the same continuous named tunnel?
check.a: No. The sheath is a short proximal fascial sleeve; the adductor canal is a separate passage farther down the thigh.

objectives: Give the boundaries and contents of the femoral triangle
Describe the femoral sheath and the femoral canal
Distinguish a femoral from an inguinal hernia
Distinguish the mid-inguinal point from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
takeaways: NAVEL from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics.
The femoral nerve is outside the sheath; the artery and vein are inside it.
A femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and strangulates easily.
The mid-inguinal point uses the ASIS and pubic symphysis; the midpoint of the ligament uses the ASIS and pubic tubercle.

title: The popliteal fossa
summary: A diamond behind the knee with the nerve most superficial and the artery deepest.

steps.title: The diamond
steps.text: Above and laterally: biceps femoris. Above and medially: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Below: the two heads of gastrocnemius. The floor is the popliteal surface of the femur, the capsule and popliteus.

check.q: Which muscles form the upper and lower borders of the popliteal fossa?
check.a: Biceps femoris and semimembranosus above; the two heads of gastrocnemius below.

steps.title: Order from the skin down
steps.text:
Superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The artery lies right on the bone, which is why it is torn by a posterior knee dislocation or a supracondylar femoral fracture, and why you check the foot pulses in both.

The common fibular nerve leaves the upper lateral angle along the biceps tendon and winds round the fibular neck – the most commonly injured nerve in the leg.

check.q: Give the order of the neurovascular structures from superficial to deep.
check.a: Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.

steps.title: Foot drop
steps.text: A fibular neck fracture, a tight plaster or prolonged crossing of the legs compresses the common fibular nerve. The deep branch supplies the dorsiflexors, so the foot drops and the patient develops a high-stepping gait; the superficial branch supplies the evertors and the skin of the dorsum.

check.q: Where does the common fibular nerve become vulnerable after leaving the fossa?
check.a: At the neck of the fibula, where it is subcutaneous.

steps.title: A swelling between two tendons
steps.text:
On the posteromedial side of the knee, a bursa lies between the medial head of gastrocnemius and semimembranosus. In many adults it communicates with the knee joint. When joint fluid distends it, the swelling is called a popliteal or Baker cyst.

Its position follows directly from the borders you have already identified. The major vessels lie deeper and more centrally, so a posterior knee swelling is not automatically a vascular structure or automatically a cyst. Anatomy supplies possible neighbours and origins; it does not establish the cause of a new lump on its own.

check.q: Between which two structures does a typical Baker cyst arise?
check.a: Semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius.

steps.title: Foot drop is a sign, not a level
steps.text:
A common fibular lesion can weaken both dorsiflexion and eversion, but tibialis posterior still inverts the foot through the tibial nerve. An L5 root lesion can involve muscles supplied through several peripheral nerves, including tibialis posterior and the hip abductors.

That gives you a comparison rather than a single-movement diagnosis. Foot drop with preserved inversion fits a common fibular pattern better; additional weakness of inversion or hip abduction suggests looking more proximally. Root overlap and incomplete lesions mean the full pattern matters more than one isolated test.

check.q: Why is tibialis posterior useful when comparing common fibular neuropathy with an L5 root lesion?
check.a: It inverts the foot through the tibial nerve but has a strong L5 contribution, so it may be affected by an L5 lesion while being spared by an isolated common fibular lesion.

objectives: Name the boundaries and contents of the popliteal fossa
Give the order of the structures from superficial to deep
Explain why a popliteal aneurysm is dangerous
Relate the posterior knee capsule and nearby bursae to a popliteal cyst
takeaways: Nerve most superficial, then vein, then artery deepest — against the joint capsule.
The common fibular nerve leaves along the medial border of biceps femoris.
The artery is tethered, so knee dislocation threatens it.
A typical Baker cyst distends the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa on the posteromedial side of the knee.

title: Gluteal region and the sciatic nerve
summary: Why the injection goes in the upper outer quadrant.

steps.title: Piriformis is the key
steps.text: Everything in the gluteal region is described relative to piriformis, which leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. The superior gluteal vessels and nerve pass above it; the sciatic nerve, the inferior gluteal vessels and nerve, the pudendal nerve and the nerve to obturator internus pass below.

check.q: Which structure leaves the pelvis above piriformis?
check.a: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels.

steps.title: The sciatic nerve
steps.text: The largest nerve in the body – L4 to S3 – descends midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, on the short lateral rotators and then on adductor magnus. It divides into tibial and common fibular branches, usually in the lower thigh.

check.q: Where does the sciatic nerve run in the buttock?
check.a: Midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.

steps.title: Safe injection
steps.text: The nerve lies in the lower medial part of the buttock, so an intramuscular injection is given in the upper outer quadrant, into gluteus medius. Damage to the superior gluteal nerve there paralyses gluteus medius and minimus and produces a Trendelenburg sign: the pelvis drops on the unsupported side when standing on the affected leg.

check.q: Which quadrant of the buttock is used for an intramuscular injection?
check.a: The upper outer quadrant.

steps.title: The skin and the hamstrings use different nerves
steps.text:
The sciatic nerve passes deep to gluteus maximus and supplies the hamstrings before its terminal branches continue towards the leg. It does not provide the main cutaneous supply to the posterior thigh. That territory belongs chiefly to the separate posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.

The two nerves emerge close together below piriformis, but proximity does not make their functions interchangeable. A lesion confined to the sciatic nerve can cause substantial weakness below the knee while sparing much of the skin over the back of the thigh. Use the model to separate where a nerve travels from what it actually supplies.

check.q: Does preserved sensation over the posterior thigh exclude a sciatic nerve lesion?
check.a: No. That skin is supplied mainly by the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, which is separate from the sciatic nerve.

steps.title: Gluteal weakness is a separate clue
steps.text:
Gluteus maximus receives the inferior gluteal nerve; gluteus medius and minimus receive the superior gluteal nerve. These branches leave the sacral plexus separately from the sciatic nerve. A nerve passing underneath a muscle need not be that muscle's motor supply.

Weak knee flexion and distal leg movement with preserved hip abduction can therefore fit a sciatic pattern. Add clear abductor weakness and the explanation may extend to the plexus, roots or a separate gluteal nerve. Compare neighbouring muscle groups to judge whether one named nerve can account for the findings.

check.q: Should an isolated sciatic nerve lesion directly paralyse gluteus medius?
check.a: No. Gluteus medius receives the superior gluteal nerve, a separate branch of the sacral plexus.

objectives: Trace the sciatic nerve through the gluteal region
Explain the safe site for an intramuscular injection
Name what leaves above and below piriformis
Distinguish sciatic motor supply from the cutaneous supply of the posterior thigh
takeaways: The sciatic nerve runs midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.
Superior gluteal above piriformis; everything else below it.
Inject into the upper outer quadrant, or the ventrogluteal site.
The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings and most of the leg and foot through its branches; posterior thigh skin mainly belongs to the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.
